title: A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how well ChatGPT can write argumentative essays compared with human-written student essays, addressing a major concern in education: whether generative AI can produce school-quality writing that challenges traditional homework and assessment practices. The authors focus on three questions: how strong ChatGPT is at writing argumentative essays, how its essays compare with student essays, and what linguistic features distinguish AI-generated from human-written text.

The study uses 90 argumentative essay topics drawn from an online forum used by German high-school students. For each topic, the researchers compared one existing student essay with new essays generated by ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 using a simple zero-shot prompt. A large group of secondary-school teachers rated the essays blind, without knowing whether an essay was human- or AI-written, using a seven-category rubric from Lower Saxony educational guidelines. The study also included computational linguistic analysis of features such as lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, nominalization, modality, epistemic markers, and discourse markers.

The population most directly involved in the empirical evaluation was 111 secondary-school teachers, mostly from German grammar schools, who produced 658 ratings across 270 essays. The student essays represented high-school-level writing, likely from grades 11–13, and were written by non-native English speakers. The rating activity occurred during an online teacher training session about ChatGPT, and participants received instructions on the questionnaire before completing the ratings.

The main conclusion is that both ChatGPT models produced essays rated significantly higher than the human student essays across all rubric criteria, with ChatGPT-4 generally outperforming ChatGPT-3.5. AI essays also showed distinctive linguistic patterns, including greater syntactic complexity and more nominalizations, while student essays used more modals and epistemic markers. The authors argue that generative AI is already strong enough to require immediate changes in educational practice, especially around homework, writing instruction, and assessment, and they recommend integrating AI into teaching in a way analogous to calculators: after foundational skills are learned, AI can be used strategically with critical reflection.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot used to generate natural-language text, here accessed via the ChatGPT web interface and representing GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 family models.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper compared argumentative essays written by students versus essays generated by ChatGPT from the same prompts/topics, and analyzed teacher ratings and linguistic characteristics of the outputs.

findings.finding_summary: Across 90 essay topics, essays generated by ChatGPT were rated significantly higher than human-written student essays on all seven rubric criteria by secondary-school teachers. For human vs ChatGPT-3, effect sizes ranged from d=0.52 to d=1.15; for human vs ChatGPT-4, effect sizes ranged from d=0.88 to d=1.43, with the largest differences in language mastery. Ratings were based on 658 total ratings of 270 essays, produced by 111 teachers.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings of argumentative essay quality on seven rubric categories: topic and completeness, logic and composition, expressiveness and comprehensiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary and text linking, and language constructs
findings.effect_size: Human vs ChatGPT-3: d=0.52 to d=1.15; Human vs ChatGPT-4: d=0.88 to d=1.43
findings.confidence_interval: 95% confidence intervals for mean values were visualized via bootstrap sampling; exact CIs not reported in text
findings.sample_size: 111 teachers; 658 ratings; 270 essays (90 topics × 3 essay types)

findings.finding_summary: Within ChatGPT outputs, the GPT-4 version outperformed the GPT-3.5 version on specific essay-quality dimensions. Significant differences were found for logic and composition (d=-0.45), complexity (d=-0.48), and vocabulary and text linking (d=-0.50), while other rubric differences were not significant.
findings.measure: Teacher ratings comparing ChatGPT-generated essays across rubric criteria
findings.effect_size: d=-0.45 (logic and composition); d=-0.48 (complexity); d=-0.50 (vocabulary and text linking)
findings.sample_size: 90 ChatGPT-3 essays and 90 ChatGPT-4 essays within the 270-essay dataset

findings.finding_summary: Linguistic analysis showed ChatGPT essays differed systematically from student essays. Compared with humans, ChatGPT used more nominalizations and greater syntactic complexity, while humans used more modals and epistemic markers; lexical diversity was lower for ChatGPT-3 than humans (d=1.06) but higher for ChatGPT-4 than humans (d=-0.60 in the table's human-vs-ChatGPT-4 comparison), with a very large difference between ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 (d=-1.93).
findings.measure: Computational linguistic characteristics: lexical diversity, syntactic complexity (depth and clauses), nominalizations, modals, epistemic markers, discourse markers
findings.effect_size: Lexical diversity: human vs ChatGPT-3 d=1.06; human vs ChatGPT-4 d=-0.60; ChatGPT-3 vs ChatGPT-4 d=-1.93; additional linguistic effects ranged from d=0.29 to d=1.53 where significant

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical comparative study with substantial sample size and rigorous scoring/statistical analysis, but it is not an RCT or QED on student learning outcomes. The study evaluates generated essay quality rather than an intervention's causal impact on learners.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects are consistently medium to very large on essay-quality ratings, with effect sizes from d=0.52 to d=1.43 for ChatGPT versus student essays. These magnitudes meet the framework's blue impact threshold, even though the outcomes are product-performance rather than student learning gains.
